title: Body and training
description: See how practice, food and recovery shape training.
author: claude

topic.title: Body and training
topic.description: Short cases from hostel rooms, gyms and hot days.

modules.title: Train, recover and read the clues

concepts.title: Progressive overload
concepts.hook: Ten clean push-ups may feel hard at first and easier after weeks of practice. What changed?
concepts.rule: Muscles adapt to repeated resistance work. For more long-term progress, the work can grow in a measured way, such as more clean reps or a harder load.

claims.text: Resistance work can build strength; a rising challenge can support further progress over time.

items.stem: In a hostel room, ten clean push-ups feel easier after a few weeks. Which change can add a fresh challenge?

options.text: Try one more clean rep.
options.feedback: A small rise in good work can give the muscles a new task after they adapt.

options.text: Keep every set the same forever.
options.feedback: The same work may still help, but a new challenge can support more progress over time.

items.stem: At a college gym, Asha adds a small load once her usual reps feel smooth. What idea is she using?

options.text: A measured rise in resistance.
options.feedback: The work gets a little harder as her ability grows, which is the overload idea.

options.text: A need to double the load each visit.
options.feedback: Progressive work can rise in small steps; a huge jump is not part of the rule.

items.stem: Two plans follow an easy set: one adds a clean rep; one repeats the same set. About how many plans raise the progressive overload challenge?

options.text: One plan.
options.feedback: The added clean rep raises the work; repeating the set keeps the task as it was.

options.text: Both plans.
options.feedback: Only one plan asks the muscles to do a bit more than before.

items.stem: What can make a familiar lift a little harder over time?

options.text: More clean reps with the same load.
options.feedback: Doing a little more sound work is one way to raise the task.

options.text: Using a new gym towel.
options.feedback: A towel can change comfort, but it does not raise the work done by the muscles.

items.stem: A trainee keeps the same easy set for months and expects that set to keep giving the same new strength gains. What is missing?

options.text: The body can adapt to that task.
options.feedback: Once work feels easier, a measured rise can offer a new reason to adapt.

options.text: The body forgets each old set overnight.
options.feedback: Practice can leave lasting change; the issue is that a fixed task may stop feeling new.

items.stem: Fill the gap: practice, adapt, then add a small new ___.

options.text: Challenge.
options.feedback: A fresh task can keep resistance work useful as the old task gets easier.

options.text: Gym badge.
options.feedback: A badge marks a visit, but it gives no new work for the muscles.

items.stem: A friend says overload means a heavier weight at every session, even when reps get rough. What needs fixing?

options.text: Progress can come from more good reps too.
options.feedback: The challenge can rise in more than one way; a forced load jump is not required.

options.text: Only a large weight jump can count.
options.feedback: A small change in sound work can also make the task harder over time.

items.stem: Put the two steps of a gradual training rise in order.

options.text: First: repeat a sound task until it feels easier.
options.feedback: Practice gives the body time to adapt before the task is raised.

options.text: Next: add a small new challenge.
options.feedback: More sound work can give the trained muscles a fresh task.

misconceptions.name: More weight every visit
misconceptions.correction: A gradual rise can use clean reps or load; every visit need not be harder.

sources.title: Resistance Training Prescription for Muscle Function, Hypertrophy, and Physical Performance in Healthy Adults

quest.title: Spot a small step
quest.detail: In a made-up training log, mark the first clean rise in reps or load.

concepts.title: Muscle, protein and rest
concepts.hook: Training gives muscle a task. Food and time between hard sessions help the body respond.
concepts.rule: Resistance work is a growth signal. Protein in food gives building blocks, and rest gives time for change. One hard session alone does not do all the work.

claims.text: The ISSN stand gives about 1.4 to 2.0 grams of protein per kilogram per day for most exercising people.

items.stem: A hostel student trains with push-ups and eats dal, curd and meals across the day. What do the meals add?

options.text: Protein that helps build new muscle tissue.
options.feedback: Resistance work is a signal, while food brings the parts the body can use to respond.

options.text: A way to skip all time between hard sets.
options.feedback: Food gives building blocks, but the body still needs time away from hard work.

items.stem: At a college gym, Dev trains hard then has a normal canteen meal with dal and rice. What is the sound link?

options.text: Food protein can support the training response.
options.feedback: The stand says a varied daily diet can meet protein needs for active people.

options.text: Only a special product can make muscles adapt.
options.feedback: The source says normal food can supply the daily protein used with training.

items.stem: For muscle training, about how many grams of daily protein per kilogram sit near the middle of the ISSN range for most active people?

options.text: About 1.7 grams per kilogram.
options.feedback: The stand gives a broad daily band from about 1.4 to 2.0 grams per kilogram.

options.text: About 7 grams per kilogram.
options.feedback: That is far above the range in the stand for most people who train.

items.stem: Which pair helps explain how resistance work can change muscle?

options.text: Training plus enough food and rest.
options.feedback: The exercise is the signal; food and time let the body respond to it.

options.text: A single hard set with no food.
options.feedback: The body needs parts from food and time to build after a hard task.

items.stem: A friend thinks adding protein to a meal can replace all resistance work for muscle growth. What part of the story is gone?

options.text: The training stimulus.
options.feedback: Protein supplies parts, while resistance work gives the muscle a reason to adapt.

options.text: The need to buy a gym pass.
options.feedback: Bodyweight work can be resistance work; a pass is not the missing step.

items.stem: Fill the gap: resistance work is a signal; food protein brings ___.

options.text: Building blocks.
options.feedback: The body uses parts from food as it responds to the work done.

options.text: An instant new muscle.
options.feedback: Growth takes repeated work and time; one meal does not make it appear at once.

items.stem: A classmate says the daily protein band is a target for every person, no matter what they do. What is the gap?

options.text: It is a range for most exercising people.
options.feedback: The stand ties that range to exercise, so it is not one rule for all people.

options.text: The stand gives one exact number for all people.
options.feedback: The source gives a range and notes that needs can vary with training.

items.stem: Match each part of muscle growth to its job.

options.text: Resistance work
options.feedback: This work asks the muscle to do a hard task and can start change.

options.text: Signal to adapt
options.feedback: A training load gives the body a reason to grow more able.

options.text: Food protein
options.feedback: Meals bring protein that the body can use as it responds to work.

options.text: Parts for new tissue
options.feedback: The body can use parts from food as it builds after training.

misconceptions.name: One part is enough
misconceptions.correction: Training, food protein and time each play a part in muscle change.

concepts.title: Sleep and recovery
concepts.hook: A late exam night can make the next run feel harder and the canteen snack more tempting.
concepts.rule: Sleep helps the body and brain recover. Too little sleep can hurt exercise output and shift hunger. One short night does not give an exact result for every person.

claims.text: Adults are advised to get about 7 to 9 hours of sleep; sleep loss can harm exercise output and hunger cues.

items.stem: After a short hostel night, Ravi starts his usual run. What might he notice?

options.text: The run may feel harder.
options.feedback: Sleep loss can hurt exercise output, though no one night fixes the same result for all.

options.text: Sleep loss must make him faster.
options.feedback: Studies link less sleep with worse exercise output on average, not a sure speed gain.

items.stem: During exams, a student sleeps less and feels more drawn to canteen snacks. Which link fits?

options.text: Sleep loss can shift hunger cues.
options.feedback: NIH notes that short sleep can change signals tied to hunger and fullness.

options.text: Sleep has no link to appetite.
options.feedback: The body uses sleep in hunger control, so a short night can change those cues.

items.stem: For sleep that supports adult recovery, about how many hours a night sit near the middle of the NIH adult range?

options.text: About eight hours.
options.feedback: The NIH page gives seven to nine hours as the usual adult range.

options.text: About four hours.
options.feedback: Four hours sits far below the range given for most adults.

items.stem: Which part of a training week gives the body time to recover?

options.text: Enough sleep and time away from hard work.
options.feedback: Sleep supports the body as it deals with the stress of exercise.

options.text: Only the hard sets themselves.
options.feedback: The sets give a task, but recovery also happens away from the session.

items.stem: A friend says one short night has no link to training because muscles only work during the session. What is missing?

options.text: Recovery and effort can change after sleep loss.
options.feedback: Sleep is part of the time when the body resets; less sleep can hurt later output.

options.text: A workout ends all need for rest.
options.feedback: The body keeps working after a session. Rest still matters on days with hard exercise.

items.stem: Fill the gap: sleep helps keep hunger and fullness cues in ___.

options.text: Balance.
options.feedback: NIH says sleep helps the signals for feeling hungry or full work together.

options.text: One fixed setting forever.
options.feedback: Those cues can shift with sleep, meals and other parts of daily life.

items.stem: A classmate reads that less sleep can hurt runs, then says every short night cuts each runner by the same amount. What is the gap?

options.text: A group trend is not one fixed personal result.
options.feedback: The review shows an average effect; people and tasks still differ.

options.text: Each runner gets an exact equal drop.
options.feedback: The studies do not turn a group result into one sure change for every runner.

items.stem: Which line best links sleep, training and appetite?

options.text: Sleep helps recovery and hunger cues.
options.feedback: Less sleep can change exercise output and the signals tied to food.

options.text: Sleep only matters during exams.
options.feedback: Sleep serves the body each day, including days with physical work.

misconceptions.name: Sleep is separate from training
misconceptions.correction: Sleep can shape rest, sport and hunger cues.

concepts.title: Heat and hydration
concepts.hook: An Ahmedabad noon can make an outdoor session feel harder than the same work on a cool day.
concepts.rule: Heat adds strain and sweat takes fluid away. On hot days, a slower pace, breaks and water help reduce heat risk. Dizziness and nausea are warning signs to stop and cool down.

claims.text: Hot exercise can raise heat risk and fluid loss. Feeling dizzy, sick or headachy can be a warning.

items.stem: A hostel run moves from dawn to hot Ahmedabad noon. Which change fits the extra heat?

options.text: A slower pace with more breaks.
options.feedback: Heat adds strain, so easing the work and taking breaks can lower heat risk.

options.text: A faster pace with no breaks.
options.feedback: Pushing harder in heat adds to the load when the body is already under strain.

items.stem: At a college cricket game in heat, a player feels dizzy and sick. What do those signs call for?

options.text: Stop play and move to a cool place.
options.feedback: CDC lists these as heat signs and says to stop activity and cool down.

options.text: Sprint once more to sweat it out.
options.feedback: More hard work can add heat when warning signs are already present.

items.stem: A hot-day mode offers three changes: slower pace, water breaks, or extra sprints. About how many help cut heat strain?

options.text: Two changes.
options.feedback: Easier work and water breaks fit the heat guide; extra sprints add strain.

options.text: All three changes.
options.feedback: Harder bursts raise effort in heat, so they do not fit a lighter session.

items.stem: Why does a hot-day session often need a lower pace?

options.text: Heat adds stress to the work.
options.feedback: The body has to shed heat while moving, so the same pace can be harder.

options.text: Heat makes fluid loss stop.
options.feedback: People can sweat more in heat and need to replace fluid they lose.

items.stem: The Train hot-day mode cuts effort and adds breaks. Why does that make sense even for someone used to exercise?

options.text: Heat and sweat add a load beyond the workout.
options.feedback: Fitness does not remove heat strain; a lower pace and breaks can help.

options.text: Regular training stops all heat risk.
options.feedback: CDC says active people still face more risk of fluid loss and heat illness on hot days.

items.stem: Fill the gap: when sweat takes fluid away, drinking water helps replace ___.

options.text: Some of that fluid.
options.feedback: Water can help cover the fluid that leaves the body as sweat.

options.text: All need for rest.
options.feedback: Water helps with fluid, but shade and breaks still matter in heat.

items.stem: A teammate says dizziness is just proof that a hot run is working. What is the gap?

options.text: Dizziness can be a heat warning sign.
options.feedback: CDC lists it among signs to stop activity and get to a cool place.

options.text: Dizziness always marks a good training load.
options.feedback: Feeling dizzy in heat is a cue to stop, not a score for effort.

items.stem: Which line best sums up the hot-day mode in Train?

options.text: Less strain, more breaks and fluid.
options.feedback: The heat guide links hot activity with fluid loss and calls for a paced effort.

options.text: More strain until warning signs fade.
options.feedback: A lighter pace is the safer link when heat has already raised the load.

misconceptions.name: Heat is a bonus workout
misconceptions.correction: Heat adds strain and fluid loss; warning signs call for a stop and a cool place.

concepts.title: Warm-up and injury myths
concepts.hook: A few easy moves before hard work can let breathing and pulse rise bit by bit.
concepts.rule: A warm-up eases the start of hard work. Static holds can help range of motion, but long holds just before a power task may dull that next effort. No stretch makes injury risk vanish.

claims.text: A gradual warm-up raises heart rate and breathing; long static holds can slightly reduce later power in tests.

items.stem: Before hostel stair sprints, Neel walks and then jogs a little. What changes first?

options.text: Pulse and breathing rise in steps.
options.feedback: An easy start lets the heart and lungs build toward harder work.

options.text: His pulse stays still until the sprint.
options.feedback: Even easy movement asks the heart and lungs to do more than rest.

items.stem: At a college gym, a friend holds one long static stretch then tries a jump test. What may happen right after?

options.text: Jump output may dip a little.
options.feedback: The review found that longer holds can trim the next power test on average.

options.text: A long hold must boost every jump.
options.feedback: Static holds can aid motion range, but the next power task may be a little weaker.

items.stem: For a warm-up before a hard run, compare two starts: easy walk then jog, or a long still hold alone. About how many ease the pulse up in steps?

options.text: One start.
options.feedback: The walk and jog raise effort in steps; a still hold does not do that job.

options.text: Both starts.
options.feedback: A static hold can change range of motion, but it is not the same gradual pulse rise.

items.stem: What is one job of an easy warm-up?

options.text: Let pulse and breath rise bit by bit.
options.feedback: The body moves from rest toward the harder task in a gradual way.

options.text: Make the hard task happen at rest.
options.feedback: An easy start prepares for work; it does not keep the body at rest.

items.stem: A coach says a long static stretch always stops injury and gives the best next sprint. Which part needs care?

options.text: Neither result is certain for every task.
options.feedback: The review finds mixed injury data and a small power dip after long holds.

options.text: A stretch makes all later work risk free.
options.feedback: One hold cannot remove all risk, and a long hold may affect the next burst.

items.stem: Fill the gap: a static stretch means holding a pose rather than moving through it ___.

options.text: Again and again.
options.feedback: A still hold is the key part of static stretching, unlike a moving stretch.

options.text: Only in the gym.
options.feedback: The name tells us how the stretch is done, not where it happens.

items.stem: A classmate hears that long still holds can dull power and says all static stretching is bad. What is missing?

options.text: Static holds can also aid motion range.
options.feedback: The effect depends on task and dose; the review does not call every hold harmful.

options.text: Every hold harms every kind of movement.
options.feedback: The source found gains in motion range and more mixed effects on other tasks.

items.stem: Which line best sums up a warm-up before hard play?

options.text: Build effort in steps and fit moves to the task.
options.feedback: A gradual start raises pulse and breath; stretch effects depend on the next task.

options.text: One long hold makes every task safe.
options.feedback: The evidence does not give one stretch that clears all risk or boosts all output.

misconceptions.name: One stretch fixes all
misconceptions.correction: A warm-up can raise effort in steps; stretch effects vary by task and dose.

concepts.title: Cardio zones and talk test
concepts.hook: A walk can feel easy while a run makes speech come in short bursts. Breath gives a clue to effort.
concepts.rule: The talk test sorts effort by speech. At a moderate pace, talking works but singing does not. At a vigorous pace, only a few words fit before a breath. These are broad effort bands.

claims.text: CDC uses talk but not sing for moderate effort, and only a few words before a breath for vigorous effort.

items.stem: On a hostel walk, Mira can chat but cannot sing a line. Which effort band fits the talk test?

options.text: Moderate effort.
options.feedback: Being able to talk but not sing is the CDC clue for this broad band.

options.text: No effort at all.
options.feedback: Speech has changed from rest, so the walk is asking the body to work.

items.stem: During college cricket drills, Arjun can say only a few words before a breath. Which band is closer?

options.text: Vigorous effort.
options.feedback: Short speech bursts before a breath match the CDC clue for hard aerobic work.

options.text: Easy rest.
options.feedback: Rest does not tend to cut speech to a few words at a time.

items.stem: Three cardio cues are easy singing, talk but not sing, and only a few words. About how many fit the moderate talk-test band?

options.text: One cue.
options.feedback: Talking but not singing marks moderate effort; the other cues point lower or higher.

options.text: All three cues.
options.feedback: The speech clues split broad effort bands, so they cannot all mean moderate work.

items.stem: What does the talk test use as a clue to effort?

options.text: How speech changes with breath.
options.feedback: As effort rises, talking and singing can become harder to keep up.

options.text: The colour of running shoes.
options.feedback: Shoe colour says nothing about how hard the heart and lungs are working.

items.stem: Two friends use the same bike speed; one can still sing and the other can only talk. Why can their effort bands differ?

options.text: The talk test tracks each person's felt effort.
options.feedback: The same outside pace can ask different amounts of work from different bodies.

options.text: A fixed speed gives all people the same effort.
options.feedback: CDC calls the test relative effort because fitness and breathing can vary by person.

items.stem: Fill the gap: at a moderate cardio pace, a person can talk but cannot ___.

options.text: Sing.
options.feedback: That speech clue is the quick rule for moderate work in the CDC guide.

options.text: Walk.
options.feedback: Walking can be moderate work; the clue is speech, not whether feet move.

items.stem: A student says the talk test proves an exact heart-rate zone number for every runner. What is the gap?

options.text: It gives a broad effort clue.
options.feedback: Speech sorts rough bands; it does not read a pulse or set one number for all.

options.text: Speech gives an exact pulse count.
options.feedback: A talk test can mark effort, but it cannot count each heart beat.

items.stem: Which line best explains the talk test to a friend?

options.text: Speech gets shorter as aerobic effort rises.
options.feedback: Talking, singing and breath gaps offer a quick way to sort rough effort levels.

options.text: Speech stays the same at every pace.
options.feedback: Breath can limit words as effort goes up, which is why the test works.

misconceptions.name: One speed fits all
misconceptions.correction: The talk test gives broad effort bands that can differ between people.

concepts.title: Habit of showing up
concepts.hook: A short hostel room session still counts as movement on a packed exam day.
concepts.rule: Some activity is better than none. Adults gain more with regular activity, and the WHO guide includes muscle work on two or more days each week. A short visit can keep a routine alive.

claims.text: WHO says some activity is better than none and advises adult muscle-strengthening work on two or more days a week.

items.stem: In a hostel exam week, Leena has time for a short bodyweight session, not her usual full one. Does it count as activity?

options.text: Yes, some movement still counts.
options.feedback: WHO says a short bout can help, even when it is less than the weekly goal.

options.text: No, only a full session counts.
options.feedback: The guide says some activity is better than none, even before a full target is met.

items.stem: A college friend trains on two steady days and skips a rare all-out day. What fits the guideline better?

options.text: Regular muscle work on two days.
options.feedback: WHO lists two or more days for muscle work; regular visits make that possible.

options.text: One huge day replaces all future work.
options.feedback: The guide gives a weekly pattern, not one burst that lasts forever.

items.stem: For an adult habit of muscle work, about how many days each week mark the WHO minimum in its activity guide?

options.text: Two days.
options.feedback: The guide sets two or more days of work for major muscle groups.

options.text: Seven all-out days.
options.feedback: The guide asks for a repeatable weekly pattern, not hard work every day.

items.stem: Which line fits the WHO guide when a person is just starting?

options.text: Some activity is better than none.
options.feedback: The guide says even a small amount of movement can have value.

options.text: Only the full target has value.
options.feedback: Benefits can begin below the target, so the first steps still count.

items.stem: A student does one very hard gym day, then no activity for many weeks, and calls the whole term covered. What is missing?

options.text: The guide describes a weekly pattern.
options.feedback: One hard day does not fill the weeks that follow with muscle work.

options.text: One day keeps giving new work forever.
options.feedback: Training gains come from work done over time, not a single day stored for a term.

items.stem: Fill the gap: a brief walk can still be worth doing because some activity beats ___.

options.text: None.
options.feedback: WHO says a little movement has value even when it does not meet the full weekly aim.

options.text: Every long walk.
options.feedback: A short walk can count without being more than all longer walks.

items.stem: A friend says two muscle days are the whole activity guide, so walking has no place. What was left out?

options.text: The guide also includes aerobic movement.
options.feedback: It pairs muscle work with time spent in moderate or vigorous activity.

options.text: Only lifting matters for all health gains.
options.feedback: The WHO guide covers both muscle and aerobic work in adult activity.

items.stem: Which line best sums up a workable training habit?

options.text: Start with some work and return to it.
options.feedback: Small bouts count. Coming back to weekly activity can help over time.

options.text: Wait until each day can be all-out.
options.feedback: The guide values some movement, so a hard perfect day is not the entry point.

misconceptions.name: Only perfect sessions count
misconceptions.correction: A short session counts. Weekly work helps when it keeps coming back.

concepts.title: Food labels in India
concepts.hook: Two snack packs can show different serving sizes. The per 100 g line gives a common base to compare them.
concepts.rule: Indian labels can show a serving size and nutrients per 100 g. A common 100 g base makes sugar and protein easier to compare across packs. Total sugar and added sugar are different lines.

claims.text: FSSAI rules list a serve size. They also list protein and sugars for a set food amount, such as 100 g or one pack.

items.stem: At a hostel shop, two snack packs use different serving sizes. Which label line gives a fair same-amount comparison?

options.text: Nutrients per 100 g on both.
options.feedback: The same mass base lets sugar or protein be compared across the two packs.

options.text: Nutrients per different listed serve sizes.
options.feedback: Different serves can hide a size gap, so those numbers lack a shared base.

items.stem: A college student reads a canteen packet with 30 g per serve and 100 g per chart line. What does 30 g name?

options.text: The stated serve size.
options.feedback: The label names the amount used for one serve, which can differ by pack.

options.text: The fixed amount in every pack.
options.feedback: Serving sizes can vary, so one pack's 30 g does not set all others.

items.stem: For food labels with unlike serving sizes, the shared FSSAI comparison line uses about how many grams of food?

options.text: 100 grams.
options.feedback: A per 100 g line puts both packs on the same food amount.

options.text: Each pack's own serving size.
options.feedback: That base can change by pack, so it is not one common amount.

items.stem: What does protein per 100 g tell a reader?

options.text: Protein in a set mass of that food.
options.feedback: The line gives the amount for one common mass, which helps compare packs.

options.text: Protein in any size of serving.
options.feedback: A serve may be more or less than 100 g, so its amount can differ.

items.stem: One snack lists more protein per serving than another but also has a much larger serve. Why check the per 100 g lines?

options.text: They put both foods on one mass base.
options.feedback: A larger serve can raise the serve number even when the food has less protein per 100 g.

options.text: The larger serve must have denser protein.
options.feedback: Serve size changes the amount counted; it does not prove a higher amount in equal food mass.

items.stem: Fill the gap: on an Indian nutrition label, total sugars and added sugars are ___ lines.

options.text: Different.
options.feedback: The label can show all sugars and the part added during food making.

options.text: Always the same.
options.feedback: A food can have sugar from its parts as well as sugar put in later.

items.stem: A student sees zero added sugar and says the total sugars line must also be zero. What is the gap?

options.text: Food may have sugars already in its parts.
options.feedback: Added sugar is one part of total sugar, so the two lines need not match.

options.text: Zero added sugar erases all other sugar.
options.feedback: The label splits added sugar from total sugar because a food can hold other sugars.

items.stem: Which line best sums up a label check for sugar and protein?

options.text: Use the same 100 g base across packs.
options.feedback: Equal food amounts let the two nutrient lines mean the same kind of comparison.

options.text: Ignore serve sizes and units on every pack.
options.feedback: The serve and the unit show how much food each number describes.

misconceptions.name: Each serve is the same size
misconceptions.correction: Serving sizes can vary; per 100 g lines give a common food amount.

sources.title: Food Safety and Standards (Labelling and Display) Regulations, 2020: compendium version VII
sources.publisher: Food Safety and Standards Authority of India
